newsitem.title: USA: Miami Nicaraguans rally against deportation threat.
newsitem.headline: Miami Nicaraguans rally against deportation threat.

text.p: Thousands of Nicaraguans, including uniformed ex-guerrillas who fought in the Contra army against the leftist Sandinistas, rallied on Sunday in a suburban Miami park to protest the threat of deportation.

Waving Nicaraguan and U.S. flags, members of Miami's exile community chanted "We want status" and applauded calls for a "humanitarian solution" to fears that the United States wants to send them back now that their homeland is a democracy.

Community leaders say Nicaraguans who have lived in south Florida for years now fear nighttime raids and deportation letters from the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service as a result of a law which tightens the process of deportation appeals and comes into effect April 1.

The rally, which organisers said attracted some 6,000 people, was reminiscent of 1980s protests when Nicaraguan exiles gathered in Miami to hear speeches from then-President Ronald Reagan and Contra chieftains urging support for the war against the Nicaragua's ruling Sandinistas.

This time, Nicaraguans were protesting attempts by the U.S. government to send them back to a democratic Nicaragua. Some waved placards reading "End Our Immigration Limbo" and "The Death and the Blood of Nicaraguans Halted the Communist Expansion to the United States."
"Fifty-thousand lie dead in Nicaragua. They gave their lives for the national security of this country," rally organiser Jose Lagos said.
Thousands fled Nicaragua in the 1980s to escape war and repression. Some were given U.S. citizenship but many, though allowed to live and work here, were denied resident status.
The U.S. government now says they must go home. Some Nicaraguans are moving from house to house and hiding with friends because they fear deportation, community leaders said.
Among those caught in the immigration quagmire are ex-guerrillas who fought in the 1980s civil war.

"I fought for my country but I fought for this country too, because the communists were taking all of Central America," said Silvano Altamirano, holding up a hand missing a finger, a wound he said was a result of fighting against the Sandinistas. "I feel like an American soldier."
At least 45,000 Nicaraguans in the Miami area are threatened by the new immigration laws, according to the exile group Fraternidad Nicaraguense.
Protesters cheered loudly when Lincoln Diaz-Balart, a Cuban-American congressman, told them a bill was pending to grant residency to Nicaraguans.

"The Nicaraguans have been treated unjustly. The reality of the matter is that they were invited here by U.S. foreign policy," he said. "The U.S. was very grateful for those who left Nicaragua as a statement against the Sandinistas."

Alfonso Aviedo, a private immigration attorney, said he would file a class-action lawsuit this week on behalf of the Nicaraguan community to halt deportations and win relief for exiles on the grounds that the United States has failed to provide them legal protection.
